speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, you will shortly see, as will all Members of the House and all Canadians, that the Ottawa-Gloucester International Airport has a new look.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT MEASURES TO ASSIST FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the federal Government has shown that it is willing to listen and ready to act for Canada's farmers. During a difficult time for the agricultural community, farmers have been justified in asking for measures of relief. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has responded personally by announcing the complete removal of all sales and excise taxes on farm fuel, a freeze on grain freight rates, an increased ceiling on domestic wheat of $11 per bushel, a fast-track approach to farm debt legislation, and Canada's role of advocacy on agriculture at the Economic Summit in Tokyo.
These measures are a clear and timely response to prairie agriculture. While we know that there is more to be done to find long-term solutions for farmers, the agricultural community can count on the Prime Minister and the Government to find the answers.

FUEL PRICE DIFFERENTIAL BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the gas price gap between Canada and the United States has widened to the extent that Canadian airlines would
rather buy their fuel in the United States. An analyst has indicated that fuel costs 20 per cent less south of the border. Burning more fuel on the way back to Canada because of full tanks is still cheaper than filling up in this country.
Again Canadians are losing money. Revenue losses on the Canadian market are recuperated by our southern neighbour because the federal Government's gas taxes are too high. The heavier the tax load, the higher the price in Canada and the longer our airlines will continue to buy American fuel. This anomaly is due to the Government whose first responsibility should be to put our country back on a competitive footing.

speechtext:

The conflict of interest guidelines provide that Ministers shall perform their official duties and so arrange their private affairs in such manner that public confidence ana trust in the integrity, objectivity, and impartiality of Government are conserved and enhanced. speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: CONFLICT OF INTEREST GUIDELINES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there is no difference in that question from those which have been asked repeatedly over the last four days. I will simply repeat to the hon. gentleman that the Code of Conduct, as it is and has been in place since September 9, 1985, requires that all Ministers comply with that code. The Minister has complied with that code, and that is a fact which he can establish for himself simply by looking at the public records with the Assistant Deputy Registrar General.

Mr. Speaker, on April 30, the Prime Minister said that there was what he called unproven and undocumented evidence. He referred it to the Assistant Deputy Registrar General who did not look at it.
